description:
## Question

Gorilla XOR-float encoding (a target workload, see "Choose the target workload set") writes a bitstream whose length depends on the data, and needs f64 <-> i64 bit reinterpretation. Kernels today return fixed-size `alloc`'d arrays. Which form fits defk: a worst-case `alloc` plus a returned bit length, a growable output buffer, a construct mirroring Elixir's `<<x::size(n)>>` building, or none (the workload ends out_of_scope)? What does each cost in the runtime (yield/resume with a partially built output) and in the one rule?

comments.text:
Resolution: the bitstring accumulator (glossary term added to CONTEXT.md).
- Form: what an Elixir developer writes first, acc = <<acc::bitstring, 1::1, 0::1, v::size(n)>>, starting from <<>>; Elixir mode is the code itself. Rejected: a worst-case [u8] with Defk.Bits.put (unidiomatic, awkward Elixir meaning); dropping Gorilla.
- Allowed: start <<>>; append integer segments v::size(n) / v::k (unsigned, MSB-first, Elixir's default); bit_size/1; return alone or in a tuple. Not allowed until a workload needs it: reading/indexing, float/binary segments, starting from an input bitstring, passing to another kernel.
- A segment value that doesn't fit its width raises, like array writes (a limit: Elixir truncates); authors mask with band. Width outside 0..64 raises (a limit). Elixir mode checks the same.
- Return: a real bitstring. The NIF returns bytes + bit length; the generated wrapper builds it with <<b::bitstring-size(len), _::bitstring>> = bin (O(1)). Padding to bytes, as Gorilla does, is an explicit append.
- Runtime: growable buffer kept in the frame across yields, freed on exception and process death (same machinery as owned arrays).
- f64 -> bits: Defk.Bits.f64_to_u64/1, a plain Elixir function whose body is <<b::64>> = <<x::float-64>>, joining the Defk.Bits set from defk-dtw.10. The match form stays in the 'Convenience constructs per workload' fog; u64 -> f64 not added (decoding isn't a target workload).
- Signature type name: bitstring, e.g. :: {bitstring, u64, i64, i64}.
Facts (gorilla_stream 3.0.3): Elixir encoder appends <<1::1, 0::1, v::size(n)>> to an iolist and calls :erlang.list_to_bitstring, masking every segment first; the C++ NIF uses an MSB-first growable std::vector BitWriter and pads to a byte at the end; worst case 77 bits per value.
Build handed off as [Add the bitstring accumulator](defk-cmr).

title: Can a kernel produce variable-length bit output, and in what form?
